newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus firms hit turbulence on company revamp.
newsitem.headline: Airbus firms hit turbulence on company revamp.

text.p: Relations between the four partners in Europe's Airbus consortium have hit turbulence, after the head of France's Aerospatiale outlined his view of the future Airbus company.

Yves Michot, chairman of Aerospatiale, last Friday told journalists the Airbus partners had agreed that Airbus would have a "management mandate", but would not own factories and design offices, once it became a joint stock company. Those assets would remain in the partners' hands.
But that vision of an asset-free Airbus conflicts with an agreement signed by the partners in January on changing the current partnership into a single corporate entity.
In London, a British Aerospace Plc (BAe) spokesman said: "BAe remains committed to the objectives of the MOU and the management of Airbus needs to control the assets."

The memorandum of understanding (MOU) said the partners had agreed to study ways of transferring assets, including factories and design offices to the new Airbus, as a first step to a wider integration of European civil and defence activities.
Airbus needs to restructure in order to boost its competitiveness and to confront a merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas of the United States.
An industry source said the MOU was an important step towards consolidation of the European aerospace industry and that the Airbus management must control assets to make it as efficient as possible.

But BAe did not want a public dispute with an Airbus partner, even though the Aerospatiale statement set it at odds with BAe and Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa), the German company in the Airbus grouping, the source added.
An executive close to Airbus Industrie disputed Aerospatiale's concept of the new Airbus and said the heads of BAe or Dasa had not accepted Michot's architecture for Airbus.
Management without control of assets was seriously flawed, he said. "Who takes the decision to close factories?" he asked of the Aerospatiale model.

The management role had been offered as just one of several scenarios by Dasa, which is forced to adopt an arm's-length approach with its Dornier subsidiary because of strained relations with the Dornier family shareholders. But it was not the last word in the Airbus restructuring talks, he said.
Airbus declined to comment.
Michot, in sketching out the new Airbus concept last Friday, said that talks subsequent to the January MOU showed that the agreement had been badly structured.

In identifying and valuing assets for the new Airbus, the partners were in danger of locking themselves into positions which could thwart a long-term restructuring of the civil and military activities, he said.

Michot cited the particular problem facing Spain's Airbus partner, Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa). Casa was a small player but had a critical mass thanks to its participation in the Eurofighter combat plane and Airbus airliners.
If Casa transferred its Airbus assets to the new Airbus, it would lose industrial volume and a commercial counterbalance to the military sector, Michot said.
But the source close to Airbus said Spain's industry minister wants Casa to split its civil and military activities into separate businesses.

Industry executives said that Aerospatiale's ability to negotiate on military matters depends on its consumating a planned merger with warplane maker Dassault Aviation, which would make it equal with BAe and Dasa.
Dassault said the merger plan was still on the agenda, after chairman Serge Dassault met the newly-appointed Communist transport minister, Jean-Claude Gayssot, on Monday.
The arrival of a Socialist government hostile to privatisations has cast grave doubts on the Aerospatiale Dassault merger, which had been ready to be announced at the Paris air show.
